summary: Specifies Cisco's Hot Standby Router Protocol, which lets hosts appear to use a single router and keep connectivity even if the actual first-hop router fails. It is informational and documents a vendor protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: HSRP lets a group of routers present one virtual router address to hosts. One router forwards traffic while a standby router monitors it and can take over if the active router fails.

how does hsrp choose an active router
subtitle: A virtual router arrangement that lets a standby router take over if the active router fails.

tldr.problem: A host with a configured default router may lose connectivity if that first-hop router fails and the host cannot discover another router dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: Routers in an HSRP group share a virtual IP and MAC address; one active router forwards traffic and a standby router can take over.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2281 documents an existing vendor protocol and notes that an IETF working group was developing a standards-track protocol for the same problem.

today: RFC 2281 is an Informational memo published in March 1998, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its IESG note says an IETF working group was then developing a standards-track protocol for the same problem.

sections.title: The Virtual Router Group
sections.content:
HSRP is designed to protect IP traffic from failure of a host's first-hop router when the host cannot learn a router dynamically. Participating routers on a multi-access LAN present the appearance of one virtual router. One router becomes active and forwards packets sent to the virtual router; another becomes the standby router.

If the active router fails, the standby router can assume forwarding duties. The RFC says HSRP is not intended to replace dynamic router discovery, which should be used when available. Multiple HSRP groups can operate on one LAN, each with its own virtual IP address and virtual MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: HSRP lets hosts send packets to one virtual router address even though several routers share the work. A standby router can start forwarding if the active router fails.

sections.title: HSRP Messages and Timers
sections.content:
HSRP messages use UDP port 1985 and are sent to multicast address 224.0.0.2 with TTL 1. A router sends its real IP address as the source address. The message fields include version, operation code, state, Hello and Hold times, priority, group, authentication data and virtual IP address.

Hello messages advertise that a router is running. Coup messages say a router wants to become active, and Resign messages say it no longer wants the active role. The memo recommends default Hello time of 3 seconds and Hold time of 10 seconds; the Hold time must be greater than the Hello time and should be at least three times as long.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers exchange Hello, Coup and Resign messages to report their state and role. Timers let them detect when messages from the active or standby router stop arriving.

sections.title: Router States and Election
sections.content:
Each router follows a state machine with Initial, Learn, Listen, Speak, Standby and Active states. A router in Learn has not determined the virtual IP address. A router in Listen knows that address but is neither active nor standby; routers in Speak participate in the election. The Standby router is the primary candidate to take over, and the Active router forwards packets for the virtual MAC address.

Priority determines the election: the numerically higher priority wins, and the higher IP address wins when priorities match. If preemption is configured, a higher-priority router may use a Coup message to become active. When a router enters Active state, it sends a gratuitous ARP response advertising the group's virtual IP and MAC addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers move through states as they learn the virtual address and take part in an election. Priority selects the active router, with the IP address breaking a tie.

sections.title: Virtual MAC Address Behavior
sections.content:
Each group has a virtual MAC address. On media other than Token Ring, the address is 00 00 0C 07 AC XX, where XX is the group number. The active router accepts and forwards traffic to this address, and stops doing so when it leaves the Active state.

Using the same virtual IP and MAC address across a takeover means host ARP entries do not need to change when the active router changes. Routers participating in HSRP must not send ICMP redirects on the interface, and proxy ARP responses must use the virtual MAC address when HSRP is supported with proxy ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: The virtual MAC address stays with the group when a different router becomes active. Hosts can continue sending to that address without learning a new router address.

sections.title: Security Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC states that HSRP does not provide security. Its authentication field can help prevent misconfiguration, but it is not a defense against an active intruder on the LAN. Such an intruder can subvert the protocol and cause a packet black hole or denial of service.

The RFC says subversion from outside the LAN is difficult because most routers do not forward packets addressed to the all-routers multicast address 224.0.0.2. The authentication data in the message is eight octets and is sent as clear text.
sections.plainLanguage: HSRP's authentication field does not protect the group from an active attacker on the same LAN. The RFC warns that an attacker can disrupt packet forwarding.

fields.name: Hellotime
fields.desc: Approximate interval between Hello messages, in seconds.

fields.name: Holdtime
fields.desc: Time a Hello remains valid, in seconds.

fields.desc: Used to elect active and standby routers.
